title: Caries with periapical findings
author: Coronation Dental Specialty Group
prompt: Identify the radiographic features indicated by the source annotation. Why are pulpal sensibility testing and clinical examination still required?
answer: The source labels deep dental decay and apical changes. Correlate with cold/EPT controls, percussion, symptoms and clinical restorability; a radiograph alone does not establish a pulpal diagnosis.

title: Ceramic crown preparation
author: EditingDentist
prompt: What preparation features should you evaluate before cementing a definitive crown?
answer: Evaluate margin continuity, sufficient reduction for selected material, retention/resistance, path of insertion, adjacent teeth, occlusal clearance, and preservation of sound tooth structure.

title: Removable partial denture
author: Matthew Ferguson 57
prompt: Differentiate retention, support and stability. What patient factors determine if an RPD design is appropriate?
answer: Retention resists displacement away from tissues; support resists movement toward tissues; stability resists horizontal forces. Evaluate abutments, periodontal status, undercuts, opposing occlusion, hygiene, and patient function.

title: Oral leukoplakia clinical photograph
author: National Cancer Institute / NIH
prompt: Describe the lesion without making a biopsy diagnosis. What features trigger referral or biopsy?
answer: Describe site, size, color, surface, whether it rubs off, induration and duration. Persistent unexplained lesions, erythroplakia, induration or ulceration warrant timely specialist evaluation and biopsy when indicated.

title: Dentigerous jaw cyst radiograph
author: Coronation Dental Specialty Group
prompt: Describe the relationship of the radiolucency to the impacted tooth. What is the appropriate diagnostic approach?
answer: The source labels a dentigerous cyst around an impacted third molar. In a new patient, document extent, cortication, displacement, resorption and relation to the crown; refer for workup and histologic confirmation where indicated.

title: Periapical film showing periodontal bone loss
author: Shaimaa Abdellatif
prompt: Identify the bone level relative to CEJs. What clinical data are needed to assign periodontitis stage and grade?
answer: Assess bone loss patterns, angular defects and possible furcation involvement. Add probing, CAL, BOP, tooth loss due to periodontitis, risk modifiers and longitudinal progression. A film alone cannot establish complete stage and grade.

title: Perio–endo lesion radiograph
author: Wikimedia Commons user Lesion
prompt: Which clinical tests differentiate a primary endodontic disease from periodontal involvement?
answer: Use pulp sensibility testing with controls, six-point probing, sinus tract tracing if present, percussion/palpation, and radiographs to identify the source and prognosis.

title: Mesioangular impacted mandibular third molar
author: Nizil Shah
prompt: What factors must be assessed before extracting this mandibular third molar?
answer: Assess angulation, depth, second-molar periodontal/caries impact, canal proximity, root form, patient age, symptoms and ability to provide care safely. Obtain additional imaging only when it changes planning.

title: Panoramic radiograph with impacted third molars
author: Coronation Dental Specialty Group
prompt: Survey the image systematically. Which findings might change surgical urgency or treatment planning?
answer: Check third-molar angulations and adjacent second molars, root formation, relationship to sinus/canal, unexpected jaw pathology and other findings; combine with clinical indications and preferences.

title: Periapical radiograph with apical radiolucencies
author: Coronation Dental Specialty Group
prompt: What pulp/apical diagnoses are plausible, and what must be tested to choose between them?
answer: The source labels an apical abscess associated with the molar. In a real case, test pulpal sensibility, percussion, palpation, periodontal probing and clinical findings before assigning specific pulpal and apical diagnoses.

title: Class II division 1 malocclusion
author: Challiyan
prompt: Which findings would you record before making an orthodontic referral?
answer: Evaluate molar/canine relationships, overjet, overbite, midlines, crowding, incisor inclination, growth, functional shift, trauma and periodontal/caries status.

title: Periodontal inflammation, calculus and caries
author: Warren Schneider
prompt: Identify plaque-retentive factors and signs of inflammation in this clinical photo. How would you prioritize care?
answer: The source describes gross caries, calculus and periodontal disease. Stabilize disease, chart periodontal findings, address risk factors, remove deposits as indicated and develop an individualized staged plan.

title: Hyrax rapid palatal expander
author: Ian Furst
topic: Transverse expansion; anchorage, tissue clearance and screw activation
prompt: Identify the molar anchorage and expansion screw. In a separate patient with palatal ulceration or band mobility, what must be checked before any further activation?
answer: Check appliance stability, screw position, tissue clearance and expansion indications. Stop unsupervised activation and arrange prompt orthodontic review for a painful or loose appliance. This credited photograph is a reference example; no defect is inferred from the photograph alone.

title: Fan-type palatal expander
author: Ian Furst
prompt: Recognize the fan hinge and why the transverse widening pattern differs from a conventional Hyrax. What errors can occur when the desired expansion pattern is not assessed?
answer: A fan-type expander can emphasize anterior expansion in selected patients. It is not a universal substitute for uniform posterior transverse expansion; monitor tooth and soft-tissue effects and use specialist/cleft-team planning when relevant. The photograph is a device reference, not proof of a defect.

title: Pendulum appliance for molar distalization
author: Challiyan
topic: Molar distalization; palatal acrylic and anterior anchorage
prompt: Which components provide distalizing force and anchorage? What happens if palatal acrylic causes ulceration or anchorage is insufficient?
answer: This is an active molar-distalization device rather than a passive space maintainer. Evaluate palatal tissue pressure, molar inclination and anchorage loss if symptoms or undesired movement occur. The photo is a reference example, not a verified malfunction.

title: Removable palatal expansion plate
author: Luis2492
topic: Removable plate; seating, clasp retention and activation
prompt: Identify the removable plate and expansion screw. What would you evaluate if the appliance does not fully seat after the patient advances the screw?
answer: Reassess force activation, retention, fit, soft tissues and whether adjustment is needed. A misfitting active appliance should not be forced into place or aggressively activated without review. The photo is a source-credited reference appliance.

title: Active removable space regainer
author: Reiherente
topic: Space regaining after premature primary tooth loss
prompt: Is this an active space regainer or a passive space maintainer? What error occurs when a child with already lost arch space receives a passive appliance instead?
answer: An active removable regainer is intended to recover some lost space when clinically feasible; a passive appliance preserves space, not regains it. Review space analysis, anchorage and monitored activation. The photo is a normal device reference.
